questions.question: What are the most important exception handling best practices in Java?
questions.title: Java Exception Handling Best Practices
questions.direct_answer: Key practices: **never swallow exceptions** (always at least log), **never catch Throwable or Exception blindly**, **log before rethrowing**, **always pass the cause when wrapping**, and **use specific exception types** that communicate the failure clearly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Code quality awareness — does the candidate write production-quality exception handling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking exception handling is just adding try-catch wherever the compiler complains
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give specific anti-patterns and the correct alternatives

sections.title: Core Best Practices
sections.content:
- **Never swallow exceptions** — empty catch {} is always wrong; at minimum log it
- **Log with the exception object** — log.error("message", e) not log.error(e.getMessage())
- **Never catch Exception or Throwable blindly** — be specific
- **Always pass the cause when wrapping** — throw new ServiceException(msg, e) not throw new ServiceException(msg)
- **Use specific exception types** — UserNotFoundException not RuntimeException
- **Don't use exceptions for control flow** — not for expected paths like 'check if user exists'
- **Clean up resources** — always use try-with-resources for I/O and connections

sections.title: Common Anti-Patterns to Avoid
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: There are a few practices I consider non-negotiable. First, never swallow exceptions — an empty catch block is almost always a bug waiting to happen. At minimum, log the exception. Second, when logging, pass the exception object itself — log.error(message, e) — not just e.getMessage(), because you want the full stack trace in the logs. Third, when wrapping an exception in a new one, always pass the original as the cause. Losing that chain makes production debugging a nightmare. Fourth, never catch Exception or Throwable blindly unless you're at the very top level of an application. These might seem obvious but I've seen all of them in real codebases.

followup_questions: What is the difference between log.error(message) and log.error(message, e)?
Why is an empty catch block always a code smell?

beats.text: Exception handling best practices are the rules that separate code that works in development from code that's debuggable in production. Most mistakes aren't about missing try-catch — they're about what you do inside catch blocks.

Poor exception handling creates invisible failures. An empty catch block makes your service appear healthy while silently dropping errors. A missing cause in a wrapped exception makes production debugging take hours instead of minutes.

questions.question: Why should you never use exceptions for control flow?
questions.title: Exceptions for Control Flow Anti-Pattern
questions.direct_answer: Exceptions are expensive — creating them involves capturing the entire **stack trace**. Using exceptions for expected conditions (like checking if a record exists) is slower than a simple if-check and semantically wrong. Exceptions should signal **unexpected exceptional conditions**, not normal program paths.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of exception performance cost and semantic intent
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using catch(NoSuchElementException) to check if a collection is empty — wrong approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain stack trace capture cost and give a concrete better alternative

sections.title: Why Exceptions Are Expensive
Key Points
sections.content:
- Exception creation captures the full stack trace — expensive on every call
- Expected/common paths should use Optional, null checks, or return values
- Exceptions for control flow: slower, harder to read, semantically wrong
- Reserve exceptions for truly unexpected conditions
- JVM cannot optimize code paths that rely on exceptions for branching

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Creating an exception in Java is expensive because the JVM has to capture the full call stack trace every time. If you're using exceptions to handle normal expected conditions — like checking if a user exists — you're paying that cost on every lookup. In a high-traffic endpoint, that adds up fast. Semantically, it's also wrong — an exception means something unexpected happened, but a user not existing is an expected case. The right approach is to return Optional from your repository and let the caller handle the present/absent case explicitly. Exceptions should be reserved for things that genuinely shouldn't happen in normal operation.

followup_questions: What is the performance cost of creating an exception in Java?
How does Optional solve the 'check if value exists' use case?
Can you suppress the stack trace to make exceptions cheaper?

When you write new Exception(), the JVM captures the complete call stack. That stack-walking is expensive. For normal control flow that happens on every request, you're paying that overhead on every execution. An if-check or Optional costs nothing by comparison.

Better alternatives — Optional for absent values, boolean return for existence checks, null-safe patterns

questions.question: What is the correct way to log exceptions in Java?
questions.title: Correct Way to Log Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: Always log with **the exception object as the second argument**: `log.error("message", e)`. Never use `log.error(e.getMessage())` — that logs only the message, losing the stack trace. Use the correct log level: error for unexpected failures, warn for expected-but-notable conditions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical logging knowledge — how to write debuggable code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: log.error(e.getMessage()) — losing the stack trace in production logs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention log levels and when to use each, plus the SLF4J parameterized logging syntax

sections.title: Logging Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- log.error(message, exception) — the exception MUST be the last argument
- The logging framework calls e.toString() and appends the stack trace
- Never use string concatenation with log messages — use {} placeholders (SLF4J)
- log.error — unexpected failures, things that need immediate attention
- log.warn — expected but notable conditions (retry attempts, fallbacks)
- log.info — significant state transitions, request handling
- log.debug — detailed diagnostic data (disabled in production)

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The correct pattern is log.error(message, e) — passing the exception as the second argument. When you pass the exception object directly, the logging framework captures the full stack trace and appends it to the log entry. If you write log.error(e.getMessage()), you only get the one-line message — in production when something goes wrong, you're left with 'NullPointerException' and no idea where it came from. Also worth mentioning: use SLF4J's parameterized logging with {} placeholders instead of string concatenation — it avoids building the string when the log level is disabled, which saves memory and CPU.

followup_questions: What is the difference between log.error(msg) and log.error(msg, e)?

questions.question: Why should you not log and rethrow the same exception?
questions.title: Log-and-Rethrow Anti-Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Log-and-rethrow** causes the same exception to be logged **multiple times** as it propagates up the call stack — each layer logs it again. This clutters logs with duplicate entries and makes log analysis confusing. You should either log OR rethrow, not both.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Logging in every catch block and then rethrowing — three layers means three log entries for the same error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the correct pattern: log once at the top (global handler), let exceptions propagate without logging

sections.title: The Log-and-Rethrow Problem
sections.content:
Imagine this call chain: Controller → Service → DAO

If each layer does `log.error + throw`:
```
[ERROR] DAO: Database failed: Connection timeout
[ERROR] Service: Failed to load user: Connection timeout
[ERROR] Controller: Request failed: Connection timeout
```

Three identical stack traces in the log for one failure. This pollutes logs and makes `grep` and log analysis tools harder to use.

**Better approach**: Let exceptions propagate silently through intermediate layers. Log once at the global exception handler (Spring's `@ControllerAdvice`). If you must log at a lower layer, do not rethrow — convert to a metric instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Log-and-rethrow causes N log entries for one error (N = number of layers)
- Log once at the outermost handler (ControllerAdvice or main)
- Intermediate layers: rethrow without logging, or catch-wrap-throw without logging
- Exception wrapping (new exception with cause) is not the same as logging — wrapping is fine
- Duplicate log entries waste storage and make alerting noisy

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Log-and-rethrow is a pattern where you catch an exception, log it, and then throw it again. The problem is that if every layer in your call stack does this, you end up with three or four identical stack traces in your logs for a single failure. That makes your logs noisy and harder to parse. The correct approach is to let exceptions propagate silently through intermediate layers and only log once at the outermost handler — in Spring, that's typically @ControllerAdvice. There's an exception to this rule: if you're wrapping the exception in a new type and you want to log at that boundary before changing the exception type, that can make sense. But logging and then rethrowing the exact same exception is almost always wrong.

questions.question: Is it bad practice to catch NullPointerException instead of fixing the null?
questions.title: Catching NullPointerException vs Fixing the Root Cause
questions.direct_answer: Yes, it's bad practice. Catching **NullPointerException** hides a programming bug rather than fixing it. The code that produces null should be fixed — through null checks, Optional, or enforcing non-null contracts — not wrapped in a try-catch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Code quality mindset — does the candidate fix problems or mask them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping code in try-catch NullPointerException when the real fix is to not have null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Optional as the modern Java approach to nulls, and Objects.requireNonNull for fail-fast validation

sections.title: Fix the Null, Don't Catch It
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Yes, catching NullPointerException is a code smell. The point of NPE is that it signals a programming bug — your code accessed something that was null unexpectedly. Catching it hides the bug rather than fixing it. The correct approach is to understand why the null appears and eliminate it at the source. If a field can be null, use Optional or add a null check before accessing it. If a parameter should never be null, use Objects.requireNonNull to throw an informative IllegalArgumentException early. The only scenario where catching NPE might be acceptable is integrating with very old third-party code that uses null in unpredictable ways — but even then, you should try to isolate and fix it.

beats.text: Catching NullPointerException is almost always a code smell. NPE signals that your code tried to use a null reference — that's a programming bug. Catching it hides the bug instead of fixing the root cause.

The temptation is to wrap risky code in catch NPE and move on. But the null came from somewhere — a method returned null it shouldn't, or a field was never initialized. Catching the symptom doesn't fix the cause, and it swallows any other NPEs in that try block too.

items: Masks the bug — the null still exists; you're just ignoring its consequences
Swallows unrelated NPEs — any NPE in the try block is caught, not just the expected one
Fix with null check — if (user != null) before accessing

beats.text: non-obvious: If you catch NPE around a block of 20 lines, any NPE anywhere in those 20 lines is silently caught. You might fix the intended null but accidentally silence a new bug introduced by a colleague two months later — with no warning.

items: Using catch NPE as a quick fix — fix the null at the source; don't mask it.
Broad try blocks with catch NPE — you'll silence unrelated null dereferences you didn't intend to catch.

questions.question: What is fail-fast and how does it relate to exception handling?
questions.title: Fail-Fast Principle in Java Exception Handling
questions.direct_answer: **Fail-fast** means detecting and reporting errors **as early as possible** — at method entry points, before processing begins. This is done with explicit validation using `if + throw` or `Objects.requireNonNull`, so errors surface immediately rather than causing confusing failures deep in the call stack.

interviewer_intent.testing: Defensive programming awareness and practical exception use
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting bad input propagate deep into the code and cause confusing NPEs far from the source
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how IllegalArgumentException and Objects.requireNonNull implement the fail-fast principle

sections.title: Fail-Fast Validation Pattern
Key Points
sections.content:
- Validate inputs at the start of a method, before any logic
- Use Objects.requireNonNull(param, message) for null checks
- Use IllegalArgumentException for invalid values (negative IDs, empty strings)
- Use IllegalStateException when the object is in a wrong state for the operation
- Fail-fast makes debugging easier — the error is close to the cause
- Without fail-fast, bad data travels deep and the error surface is far from the real problem

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Fail-fast means you validate your inputs at the very start of a method and throw immediately if they're invalid. The idea is that if bad data enters a method, you want to know right there — not three levels deep when some unrelated operation fails with a cryptic NullPointerException. In Java, you implement this with Objects.requireNonNull for null checks and IllegalArgumentException for invalid values. So at the top of your method, you check: is this ID null? Is it positive? If not, throw immediately with a clear message. This makes debugging much easier because the exception and the bad input are right next to each other in the stack trace.

speakable_v2.hook: Fail-fast means throwing the moment bad data enters your method — not three layers later when a cryptic NPE appears far from the real problem.

beats.text: Fail-fast is a defensive programming principle: validate all inputs at the start of a method and throw immediately if they're invalid. The exception occurs at the exact point where bad data enters, making the stack trace directly useful instead of misleading.

Without fail-fast, a null ID passed to findById() might cause a NullPointerException twenty lines later inside a JDBC query builder. The stack trace points to the query builder, not the null — debugging requires tracing back to the original bad call.

items: Objects.requireNonNull(param, msg) — throws NullPointerException with a clear message if param is null
IllegalArgumentException — for invalid values (negative IDs, empty strings, out-of-range numbers)
IllegalStateException — for when the object is in the wrong state for the operation
Validate at method entry — before any business logic runs

beats.text: non-obvious: Objects.requireNonNull throws NullPointerException, not IllegalArgumentException — even though null is arguably an illegal argument. That's by design; Java conventions distinguish between null-specific validation (NPE) and other invalid values (IAE). Always use requireNonNull for null, IAE for everything else.

items: Validating in the middle of a method — check at entry before any side effects happen.
Using IllegalArgumentException for null — use Objects.requireNonNull instead; conventions matter in code reviews.

speakable_v2.cap: Validate at method entry with requireNonNull and IllegalArgumentException — surface bad input immediately, not three layers later.
